## The last paper you cited

How much of it did you read?

And the AI summary, if there was one: did it come

::: {.incremental}
- **before** your reading,
- **after** it,
- or **instead** of it?
:::

::: notes
Ask for hands on each of the three. Don't comment on the split yet, and don't treat any answer as the wrong one. The point is to notice which one it was.

Keep the three words in mind: before, after, instead. They are the whole argument of this talk in miniature. The protocol at the end puts AI before your own reading and after it, and never instead of it.

Everything between here and there is the case for that: what the classic reading guides say, how the AI tools map onto them, what the evidence says about how researchers use the tools, and where the tools fail.
:::

## The advice is old; the assistant is new

The classic guides agree on three things:

- read **in layers**, not front to back once
- read **with a goal**, set before you start
- **verify by reconstruction**

What has changed: AI can now **do** the first layer, **tutor** you through the second, and **argue** with you after the third.

::: notes
The classic guides were all written before an assistant could summarize, explain or critique a paper. Their advice still holds.

The layers matter most. A paper is not read front to back, once. You make several passes, each deeper and more expensive than the last, and you decide before you start what you want from the paper.

Field-specific guides for mathematics, statistics, CS, computational biology and neuroscience change what you read closely on each pass. They don't change the layers.

So the question for the rest of the talk is narrow: which layers can you hand to an assistant, and which stay yours?
:::

## Keshav's three passes

| Pass | Time | What you read |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5–10 min | title, abstract, intro, headings, conclusions |
| 2 | ~1 h | the figures and the argument; skip the proofs |
| 3 | — | virtually re-implement the work |

After pass 1, answer the **five Cs**: category, context, correctness, contributions, clarity.

[Keshav, "How to Read a Paper", 2007]{.source}

::: notes
Keshav's three passes are the skeleton the later guides share.

Pass one is five to ten minutes on the paper's outline. It ends with the five Cs: what category of paper this is, what context it sits in, whether its assumptions look correct, what it contributes, and whether it is clearly written. That is enough to decide whether to keep going.

Pass two is about an hour with the figures and the argument, skipping proofs.

Pass three is a virtual re-implementation: you rebuild the work in your head, or for real, and compare your version with theirs. That is where errors and hidden assumptions turn up.

The same guide also gives a recipe for a literature survey, which matters for Pass 0 later.
:::

## Every guide shares the skeleton

| Guide | What it adds to the passes |
|---|---|
| Carey, Steiner & Petri (2020) | pick a reading goal first; read the figures before the text; question each panel; afterwards ask "now what?" |
| Mensh & Kording (2017) | a writing guide whose context–content–conclusion model tells a reader where each claim lives |
| Leek group (2016) | a working statistician's own process, kept as an open GitHub guide |

The later guides change **what** you read on each pass, not the layered structure.

[*PLOS Computational Biology* (Carey et al.; Mensh & Kording); github.com/jtleek/readingpapers]{.source}

::: notes
Three more general guides, all compatible with Keshav.

Carey and colleagues' ten simple rules, written for biology, start with a goal: decide why you are reading before you read. Then figures before text, questioning each panel, and at the end asking "now what?" and connecting it to your own science.

Mensh and Kording wrote a guide to structuring papers, but read in reverse it tells you where each claim lives in a well-built paper: context, content, conclusion.

Jeff Leek's group keeps a statistician's reading process as an open guide on GitHub, alongside his guides to reviewing.

None of them replaces the layers. They change what you attend to inside each one.
:::

## Fields change the unit of attention {.smaller}

| Field | Unit of attention | Read closely for |
|---|---|---|
| Mathematics | theorems | test every claim with an example; skim a proof for the idea, go line by line, then summarize |
| Statistics | design and inference | the estimand; causal or observational; how many comparisons; effect size with uncertainty; code and data |
| CS and ML | claims against evidence | baselines, compute budgets, ablations, seeds; is the benchmark contaminated |
| Computational biology | figures and data | the figures first; is the code public and runnable; which versions, parameters and thresholds |
| Neuroscience | analysis pitfalls | low power; "double dipping"; two significance tests compared instead of testing the interaction |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20,20,60]"}

[Simonson & Gouvêa; Schwer 2026; Khovanova 2026; Greenhalgh; Ng 2019; Carey et al. 2020; Mensh & Kording 2017]{.source}

::: notes
Each field shifts what you read closely. The layers stay the same.

Mathematics reads slowly, in hours per page rather than pages per hour. Test every claim with a small example. For proofs, Schwer's recent guide says: skim for the idea, then go line by line, then summarize. Khovanova iterates up to six reads to learn a paper deeply.

Statistics: what is the estimand, the quantity the study sets out to estimate? Is the design causal or observational, how many comparisons were made, and is the effect reported with uncertainty?

ML: baselines, compute, ablations, seeds, and benchmark contamination.

Computational biology: figures first, then the computational layer. Could the result survive a different pipeline?

Neuroscience has no single canonical guide, so its methods-critique papers serve as the checklist.
:::

## The tools, by job {.smaller}

| Job | Examples | Main caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Discover and map a field | Semantic Scholar, Connected Papers, ResearchRabbit, Undermind | coverage gaps; ranking favors highly cited work |
| Synthesize many papers | Elicit, Consensus, OpenScholar, PaperQA2, research modes | fabricated or mismatched citations; overgeneralized claims |
| Read one paper with help | alphaXiv, Semantic Reader, SciSpace, NotebookLM | summaries flatten caveats and hedges |
| Check citation context | scite | classifier errors on nuanced citations |
| Verify math and code | assistants with code execution; Lean for formal checks | confident but wrong derivations unless formally checked |

: {tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

The tools are strongest at **triage and navigation**, and weakest at **judging whether a result is right**.

::: notes
The AI tools now cover every stage Keshav describes, from finding papers to interrogating a single equation.

Read the caveat column more than the examples. Product rankings in this space change monthly, but the failure modes are stable. Discovery tools favor highly cited work. Synthesis tools can fabricate or mismatch citations and overgeneralize. One-paper tools flatten hedges. Citation classifiers miss nuance. Derivations come back confident and wrong unless something formal checks them.

The pattern is that the tools are good at the shallow, wide layers, finding and navigating, and weak at the judgment layer, deciding whether a result is right. That asymmetry is what the protocol at the end is built on.
:::

[Semantic Scholar lists 248 papers citing Keshav (2007). 45 of them predate it, and 157 are tagged Medicine.]{.graph-note}
:::
::::

[Semantic Scholar Graph API, snapshot of 2026-10-10; Connected Papers, "About"]{.source}

::: notes
This is Semantic Scholar's own record for Keshav's paper, taken as a snapshot. Each sphere is a paper the API lists as citing Keshav, sized by its citations and coloured by Semantic Scholar's field tag. Height is the year; the floor is 2007.

First click: a citation can only point back in time, so every link should run down to Keshav. The arrows run up. Across the whole record, 45 of the 248 citing papers predate Keshav's, and 157 are tagged Medicine against 68 Computer Science. The likeliest explanation is a same-title mix-up: several works are called "How to Read a Paper", Greenhalgh's among them.

Second click: shared references, or bibliographic coupling, one of the two measures Connected Papers says its similarity is built from. Most of these links join papers that never cite each other. Here they join medical papers.

Third click: rank the citing papers by their own citations, and all five at the top are medical papers. None of the five is among the five best connected, so a citation ranking and a connection map send you to different papers.

A map is a triage tool, and it needs the same checking as anything else. It is also incomplete: the API returned reference lists for only a minority of the citing papers.
:::

## Retrieval-grounded tools invent far fewer citations

::: {.nums}
::: {.num}
[~78–90%]{.v}
[of citations fabricated by a general model (GPT-4o) in OpenScholar's tests]{.l}
:::
::: {.num}
[near experts]{.v}
[OpenScholar's citation accuracy, answering from 45 million open-access papers]{.l}
:::
::: {.num}
[~50–70%]{.v}
[of the time, experts preferred its answers over expert-written ones]{.l}
:::
:::

Use tools that **retrieve and cite** real documents, and **click through** every citation that matters.

[OpenScholar, *Nature*, February 2026 (Nature Asia press release)]{.source}

::: notes
The most rigorous evidence so far is for retrieval-grounded systems. OpenScholar, published in Nature in February, answers questions from a store of 45 million open-access papers.

In its tests, a general model, GPT-4o, fabricated citations roughly 78 to 90 percent of the time. OpenScholar's citation accuracy approached that of human experts, and experts preferred its answers over expert-written ones about 50 to 70 percent of the time.

The practical lesson is not "use OpenScholar". It is to use tools that retrieve and cite real documents, and then open every citation that matters, because "approached human experts" is still not zero errors.

Opening a citation means more than checking that the paper exists. A mismatched citation is a real paper that doesn't say what the answer claims it says, so read the sentence being cited.
:::

## AI reading moves fastest in peer review

::: {.nums}
::: {.num}
[over half]{.v}
[of reviewers now use AI when reviewing, up from 24% in 2024]{.l}
:::
::: {.num}
[61% · 45%]{.v}
[early-career against senior researchers]{.l}
:::
::: {.num}
[77% · 31%]{.v}
[China against North America]{.l}
:::
:::

Top uses: writing the report (59%), summarizing the article's findings (29%), flagging possible misconduct (28%).

Across almost 5,000 researchers, 63% cite unclear guidelines or lack of training as barriers.

[Frontiers survey of about 1,600 researchers, reported January 2026 (NISO); Wiley ExplanAItions, 2025 (NISO)]{.source}

::: notes
AI-assisted reading is now mainstream, and it is moving fastest in peer review, where reading closely is the job.

A Frontiers survey of about 1,600 researchers found over half now use AI when reviewing, up from 24 percent in 2024. Use runs higher among early-career researchers than senior ones, and varies by region.

Look at the top uses. The most common is writing the report, not reading the paper. Summarizing the article's findings is second, which is exactly the use the next slides warn about.

Wiley's study of almost 5,000 researchers found use still fairly narrow in tools and tasks, and 63 percent cite unclear guidelines or lack of training as barriers.
:::

## Four workflows that have emerged

- **Triage at scale.** Ask for the five Cs of each of 30 candidate papers, then pick five to read yourself.
- **Tutor on demand.** Paste an unfamiliar method section; ask for the prerequisites, a worked toy example, or the notation decoded.
- **Adversarial second reader.** After your own pass, ask for the weakest assumption, missing controls or alternative explanations. Judge those yourself.
- **Reproduction partner.** Re-implement an analysis or re-derive an equation with it: Keshav's virtual re-implementation made literal.

[AI before and after your own reading, not instead of it.]{.punch}

::: notes
Four workflows have emerged, and they line up with the layers.

Triage sits before your reading. It is Keshav's first pass, done at scale: thirty papers' five Cs, and you choose five to read. The arithmetic is the attraction. At about two minutes a paper, thirty papers take an hour. Thirty first passes by hand, at five to ten minutes each, take two and a half to five hours.

Tutoring sits inside the second pass. The model explains; you are still the one reading.

The adversarial reader comes after your own pass. Order matters here: your own reading comes first, then the model's objections, which you judge.

The reproduction partner turns the third pass from a thought experiment into a literal one.

None of the four replaces your reading. Each one sits before it, inside it, or after it.
:::

## Risk: summaries overstate findings

::: {.nums}
::: {.num}
[nearly 5×]{.v}
[likelier to overgeneralize than expert-written summaries of medical papers]{.l}
:::
::: {.num}
[10 · 4,900]{.v}
[models tested · summaries compared]{.l}
:::
::: {.num}
[worse]{.v}
[some newer models; and asking to "avoid inaccuracies" made it worse still]{.l}
:::
:::

**What to do:** read the abstract's hedges and the limitations section yourself. Ask the model to **quote the exact sentence** behind each claim.

[Peters & Chin-Yee, *Royal Society Open Science*, 2025 (PsyPost)]{.source}

::: notes
The three failure modes to plan around are distorted summaries, invented sources, and the slow loss of your own reading skill.

Distorted summaries first. Peters and Chin-Yee tested 10 models on 4,900 summaries. Model summaries of medical papers were nearly five times likelier to overgeneralize than expert-written ones. Some newer models were worse than older ones, and asking the model to avoid inaccuracies made it worse still.

So a careful prompt is not the fix on its own. The fix is procedural: read the hedges and the limitations yourself, and make the model quote the sentence its claim rests on, so you can check the claim against the text.

This is the medical-paper version of a caveat we saw on the tools slide: summaries flatten caveats and hedges.
:::

## Three more risks {.smaller}

| Risk | Evidence | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Fabricated or mismatched citations | general models invented most citations in the OpenScholar tests | use retrieval-grounded tools; open every citation you will rely on or repeat |
| Deskilling and shallow understanding | MIT's "Your Brain on ChatGPT" preprint (small sample, essay writing): lower neural engagement, weaker recall; Schwer warns of the same trade-off | do the first pass and the hard parts (proofs, derivations, figure reading) unaided; use AI to check, not to replace, that work |
| Confidentiality | uploading an unpublished manuscript you are reviewing may breach journal policy | check the journal's AI policy before using any tool on a manuscript under review |

: {tbl-colwidths="[22,42,36]"}

[OpenScholar, *Nature* 2026; "Your Brain on ChatGPT", MIT Media Lab preprint; Schwer 2026]{.source}

::: notes
Invented citations we have seen. The response is retrieval-grounded tools, and opening every citation you will rely on or repeat.

Deskilling is the slow one. The MIT preprint is a small sample and about essay writing, not paper reading, so hold it loosely. But it found lower neural engagement and weaker recall in the assisted group, and Schwer's 2026 guide to reading mathematics warns of the same trade-off. The protection is to keep the hard parts, the proofs, the derivations and the figure reading, for yourself.

Confidentiality is the easy one to get wrong when reviewing. Uploading an unpublished manuscript you are reviewing may breach journal policy, so check the policy before using any tool on it.
:::

## The three passes, updated for AI

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
::: {#layers-ai .pl-mount}
:::
:::
::: {.column width="42%" .pl-steps .pl-steps-dense}
::: {.fragment .step data-pass="0"}
**Pass 0 · triage** [AI · ~2 min a paper]{.meta}<br>candidates and their five Cs; set your reading goal
:::
::: {.fragment .step data-pass="1"}
**Pass 1 · bird's-eye view** [you · 5–10 min]{.meta}<br>every figure too; your own one-sentence summary before any AI summary
:::
::: {.fragment .step data-pass="2"}
**Pass 2 · the argument** [you, AI as tutor · ~1 h]{.meta}<br>each claim and its evidence
:::
::: {.fragment .step data-pass="3"}
**Pass 3 · deep read** [you · hours]{.meta}<br>the checks your field asks for
:::
::: {.fragment .step data-pass="4"}
**Pass 4 · adversarial check** [AI, then you]{.meta}<br>demand quoted evidence; verify citations
:::
::: {.fragment .step data-pass="integrate"}
**Integrate** [you]{.meta}<br>what it claims, how far you believe it, what next
:::
[ ]{.sw .sw-you} you  [ ]{.sw .sw-ai} AI · fill leads, edge seconds
:::
::::

::: notes
Same paper, same layers, now with AI in it. Purple is you, amber is AI. A sheet's fill is whoever leads that pass and its edge is whoever seconds it.

Pass zero is new. A retrieval-grounded tool reads the top sheet of many papers, wide and shallow. Set your goal before going further.

Pass one is yours, and now includes every figure. Write your own one-sentence summary before you read any AI summary, then compare the two.

Pass two is yours, with AI as tutor for methods, notation and prerequisites.

Pass three is yours alone: the bottom of one paper, narrow and deep.

Pass four is the skeptic: the AI looks for the weakest assumption, missing controls and alternative explanations, with quoted evidence, and you verify any citation you will rely on. Then you judge.

Integrate: a short note in your own words.

Compare this with the classic version a few slides back. AI has been added at both ends, and the middle has not changed hands. Pass three and the note are purple in both pictures.
:::

## Pass 3, by field

- **Math:** work small examples; re-prove the key lemma; formalize one step if it matters.
- **Statistics:** identify the estimand, design and multiplicity; re-run the analysis if data exist.
- **CS and ML:** check baselines, ablations and compute; re-implement the core method.
- **Computational biology:** run the pipeline, or at least audit versions and parameters.
- **Neuroscience:** check power, circular analysis and interaction tests.

::: notes
The deep pass is where the field-specific guides earn their place, and it is the pass that stays yours.

In mathematics, re-proving the key lemma is the reconstruction, and formalizing one step in a proof assistant such as Lean is the check that does not rest on trust: derivations come back confident and wrong unless something formal checks them.

In statistics, the estimand, the design and the multiplicity come first, then a re-run if the data exist.

In ML, the core method is re-implemented. An assistant can help write that code, but you decide what counts as a fair baseline.

In computational biology, run the pipeline or audit its versions and parameters.

In neuroscience, check power, circular analysis and interaction tests.
:::

## {.closer}

AI before and after your own reading, not instead of it.

[Read. In. Layers.<br>AI. Triages. Tutors. Argues.<br>You. Judge.]{.coda}

::: notes
Back to the opening question: before, after, or instead.

Keep Keshav's structure. Add an AI-assisted pass zero in front and an adversarial pass four behind. Keep the judgment passes yours.

Read in layers. AI triages, tutors and argues. You judge.

A concrete next step: try the protocol on the next paper you read closely. If it is one you are reviewing, check the journal's AI policy before any tool sees it.
:::
